summary: Initial discovery to map Alexia Insights' latency SLOs, monthly budget constraints, and feasibility of a hybrid hosting path (hosted for burst + dedicated for baseline). Focus on per-token economics, batching/caching levers, and pilot success criteria. Action items: pricing spreadsheet, pilot harness, sample prompts, security review.
transcript:
[00:00] Samir: Alright everyone, uh, thanks for joining. I think we have about 45, 50 minutes. Quick intros?
[00:07] James: Hi, James Lee, CTO at Alexia, I'm leading their platform and infra decisions.
[00:11] Priya: Priya Rao, Head of ML, I own the recommender and conversational features.
[00:14] Marcus: Marcus Chen, product, I own the user-facing chat flows.
[00:17] Samir: Great. I'm Samir, AE at Redwood, and with me is Clara, our solutions engineer. Clara, quick wave?
[00:22] Clara: Hey all. We'll probably dive into some perf and cost details — happy to take that.
[00:28] [00:30] Samir: High level, Alexia — tell us what's driving this exploration. What are the must-haves and the constraints?
[00:35] James: Sure. We're launching an assisted analytics feature; it will be high QPS during daytime in NA, and we need both very predictable monthly spend — the CFO set a hard run rate cap — and sub-200ms token latency for some of the interactive flows. We're also sensitive about data residency, we keep PII in our VPC.
[00:52] Priya: To add, we expect mixed traffic: short context Q&A (100-200 tokens) and longer generation jobs for batch reports (2k tokens). The short flows are the priority for UX.
[01:05] Samir: Got it. So two axis: latency SLO for interactive, and cost/run-rate cap. How are you currently serving models?
[01:12] James: We have an internal Triton-based setup for embeddings and small models. For LLM, we've been proofing with a managed API — a few prototypes on, uh, a large LLM provider. But cost scaled really badly. We want an ops-lite solution but with deterministic cost.
[01:27] Samir: Right, that's familiar. Clara, do you want to frame how Redwood approaches per-token economics and the main levers?
[01:33] Clara: Sure. There are a few things folks use: first is hosting mode — hosted pay-as-you-go is simplest but per-token costs are higher; dedicated reserved capacity gives flat monthly capacity and lower per-token costs for steady traffic. Second is batching — we can batch requests to amortize GPU overhead which lowers tokens-per-second cost but can add latency. Third is caching — prefix/KV cache for conversations can reduce tokens actually processed per request. Then quantization/ model choice — smaller quantized variants can be cheaper per token, and routing/policy lets you fall back to cheaper variants for non-critical calls.
[02:05] [02:10] Marcus: That batching vs latency tradeoff — can you get sub-200ms with batching?
[02:15] Clara: It depends. If you have very low tail-latency budget, continuous batching that waits even 10–20ms can push you over. For sub-200ms interactive, what people do is keep batch windows small and prioritize low-latency queueing on dedicated pools. Also prefix caching can chop off a bunch of tokens before the forward pass.
[02:31] Priya: We're curious about realistic numbers. For our 150-token average interactive, what does per-token look like hosted vs dedicated?
[02:38] Samir: I'll give a ballpark — these are workload-dependent — but hosted might be in the X¢/token range for that throughput, whereas dedicated can drop that 30–60% depending on utilization and model family. I'll send a detailed worksheet with scenario modeling.
[02:52] [03:00] James: Can you explain utilization assumptions? Our traffic is spiky; peaks are 4x baseline during business hours.
[03:07] Clara: Sure. For dedicated, you size for baseline and use autoscale burst for peaks. If baseline utilization is low, your effective per-token cost goes up because GPUs idle. So you decide whether to reserve more to lower per-token for steady traffic or keep a small dedicated baseline and rely on hosted bursts — a hybrid mix.
[03:24] Marcus: Is hybrid common?
[03:26] Clara: Very. Many customers run a dedicated pool for core users and route overflow to hosted or cheaper model families. Redwood's smart routing can split by latency-sensitive vs cost-sensitive traffic.
[03:37] [03:40] Priya: You mentioned caching — specifically KV cache. How often does that reduce token count in practice for conversation flows?
[03:46] Clara: For multi-turn chats with shared system and user prefixes, we've seen effective token reduction of 20–60% depending on prompt design. If you precompute embeddings or use summaries, it can be higher. But you need to plan for cache invalidation and privacy — if prompts include PII, residency rules matter.
[04:03] James: About residency — we need message content never to leave our VPC. That pushes us to Private deployment, right?
[04:10] Samir: Not always. You can do Private deployment (VPC/on-prem) which keeps inference inside your network, or you can use Hosted/Dedicated with encryption and contractual controls depending on compliance requirements. For strict PII rules, Private is common. For many customers we do dedicated private control plane plus customer-managed VPC peering.
[04:26] [04:30] Priya: Okay. For pilot scope — if we run a 3-week pilot, what should we provide to get valid unit economics?
[04:37] Clara: Provide representative prompt sets, distribution of sequence lengths, concurrency/QPS profile, and any system messages. We'll run benchmarks with your prompts against the model variants and produce a per-token burn simulation with caching/batching knobs. We'll also run latency percentiles.
[04:51] Samir: And we'll include a few scenarios: hosted-only, dedicated baseline + hosted burst, and private deployment cost.
[04:58] [05:00] James: How do you price dedicated? Is it flat GPU commit + usage?
[05:06] Samir: It's usually a monthly reserved pool price (capacity commit) and a lower per-token charge for additional tokens. Think of it as committed capacity for predictable throughput. There are also options for burst capacity and overage policies.
[05:18] Marcus: In terms of model variants — are you recommending smaller models for certain flows?
[05:21] Clara: Exactly. For retrieval-augmented Q&A where we do short answers, a mid-sized quantized model might be indistinguishable to users and much cheaper. For long creative generation, you may need the full model. Routing lets you match models to intent.
[05:36] [05:40] Priya: Any gotchas around batching with our existing front end? We have tight per-turn SLOs and single-turn retries can be expensive.
[05:46] Clara: The main thing is to set client-side timeouts and let the runtime prioritize low-latency lanes. Also, idempotency keys and dedupe logic help to avoid double token charge on retries. We'll share best-practice patterns in the pilot docs.
[05:59] James: Security checklist — SSO, SAML, audit logs, KMS integration — do you support all of these for Private?
[06:07] Samir: Yes for Private we do SAML/SSO, RBAC, KMS/HSM integrations for key control, and audit logs with retention options. For Dedicated hosted we can enable many of these features too, but if you need full network isolation and customer-managed key material, Private is the path. We'll include our security pack link in the follow-up.
[06:24] [06:30] Marcus: What about regression monitoring? If we change model family for cost reasons, how do we avoid quality drops?
[06:36] Clara: Redwood Optimize ties model rollouts to eval suites. You can pin an eval and get alerts for quality regressions on a prompt set. For pilot we can run A/B comparisons against your golden prompts.
[06:46] [07:00] Samir: Let me anchor some numbers — Clara will provide the bench numbers — but operationally customers using dedicated often see 30–60% lower tokens cost at high utilization, but you need to be comfortable with commit sizing. Hybrid tends to smooth that.
[07:15] James: We're nervous about committing given our product roadmap; can commit size be adjusted mid-contract?
[07:20] Samir: Contracts have scaling windows; we can build in a step-up cadence and include shorter notice periods for scale. We often do 6–12 month commitments with quarterly adjustments.
[07:30] [07:35] Priya: For the pilot, what success criteria should we set so finance signs off?
[07:40] Marcus: From product side I'd say: 95th perc latency under 250ms for interactive flows, cost per 1K queries under $X (TBD once we see model choice), and no data residency violations.
[07:52] Samir: Perfect — we'll translate those into the pilot worksheet.
[07:56] [08:00] James: One more: fallbacks. If you have a region failure, how do you keep service available without exploding cost?
[08:07] Clara: Redwood supports multi-region routing and automatic fallbacks to compatible model variants. You can set policies to prefer same-region and failover to a cheaper variant in another region. There's also an auto-fallback to hosted from dedicated for short outages.
[08:20] [08:25] Marcus: Any rough lead time to get dedicated up and running for pilot?
[08:28] Clara: For a pilot we can spin up a dedicated pool in a week if capacity's available; Private deployments take longer — usually a few weeks to coordinate networking/KMS and security review.
[08:39] Samir: Alright we're nearing the last 10. Quick recap and next steps.
[08:44] [08:50] Samir: Action items — I'll send the pricing spreadsheet and a few scenario tabs (hosted vs dedicated vs hybrid) with example math. Clara will prepare the benchmark harness and a short doc on batching/caching tradeoffs. James/ Priya will share prompt set and traffic profile. We'll aim to kick the pilot week of 11/22 or 11/29.
[09:04] James: Sounds good. Also please include the security pack and SOC2 evidence.
[09:08] Samir: Will do. We'll include SAML/KMS notes and proposed dates for a security review.
[09:12] Priya: One tiny thing — can you include a column in the spreadsheet showing tokens processed after prefix caching? That helps our finance person.
[09:18] Clara: Yes we'll add a cached tokens column and an assumed cache hit rate slider so you can play with it.
[09:24] Marcus: Ok thanks.
[09:26] Samir: Thanks everyone. We'll follow up within two business days.
[09:30] [END]
